title: Ang 469–475: Asa di Var, second half
hookLine: sweetness, humility and the thread of compassion
tomorrow: who stretched the whole world out on a loom?

lines: THE BRACELET YOU FORGET YOU WEAR.
cards: Thread bracelets are everywhere: the band from summer camp, the string someone tied on a wrist, the one worn so long it's forgotten. Threads fray, though. They snap in the wash.
On ang 471, Guru Nanak describes one that doesn't. In paraphrase: it doesn't break, doesn't get dirty, doesn't burn, doesn't get lost.

teach.b: He spins it from virtues, in paraphrase: make compassion, daya, the cotton; contentment, santokh, the thread; self-control the knot; truth the twist. That's a thread for the soul, and whoever wears it is blessed.
A page earlier, on ang 470, the same Asa di Var names what holds every good quality together: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence. So, today's question: what's worth wearing?
Here's how a neighbor tradition answers.
In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Micah asks what the LORD requires, and answers, in the 1917 Jewish translation: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.”
Mercy and humility, in Micah's words; compassion and humility, in Guru Nanak's. That's real common ground. And an honest difference.
Micah speaks as a prophet of Israel's God and names what is required: a command, in the covenant language of his people.
Guru Nanak gives a picture instead: something you spin from your own virtues and wear, a thread for any soul.
One is a requirement, one is a garment.
Both ask for mercy and a low, sweet heart.

how: The second half of Asa di Var is sung at the morning kirtan in gurdwaras and read in order in Raag Asa; the saloks on sweetness and humility and on the thread of compassion are among its lines Sikhs return to.

o: where the second half of Asa di Var picks up
where Asa di Var, the dawn ballad, starts

s: Guru Nanak's thread is spun from cotton from a field
compassion is the cotton, contentment the thread, self-control the knot, truth the twist.
Micah's answer includes loving mercy and walking humbly
to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.
Micah and Guru Nanak say exactly the same thing
both prize mercy and humility; Micah names what the LORD requires, Guru Nanak pictures a thread to wear.

games.q: a classmate posts every hour he spends volunteering. you volunteer quietly. a friend says, call him out. what fits the thread?
o: keep giving with sweetness, and don't sneer at him either.
start posting too, so people know you're just as good.
call him out publicly for showing off.
games.why: sweetness and humility are the essence, says ang 470: for your own giving, and for how you see his.

practice: Read ang 470 first if you can. If something sweet is nearby, a raisin, a bit of honey, a sip of chai, taste it slowly and let the sweetness last.
If not, hold a piece of thread or string and run it through your fingers, and rest with one word: sweetness.

wordCard.voice: Ang 469. The page where the second half of Asa di Var carries on, toward the thread of compassion.

carryVoice: Worth keeping: the thread, spun from compassion and worn on the inside. See you tomorrow.
